DevWorkspace — User guide
Windows x64 · English

01. Installation and preparation

DevWorkspace is a Windows x64 desktop workbench. It works alongside your existing IDE and terminal, so you can keep your development tools.

1. Choose the Windows installer in the website’s Download section. For portable use, download and extract the ZIP package.
2. Open the application and follow the getting-started guide. Reopen it later from Help → Getting started.
3. New installations start in English. Change the language in Settings if you prefer Turkish; existing preferences are retained.
4. Check the tools you need under Help → Development tools. Git, GitHub CLI, SDKs, Docker and the security scanner are required for their respective features.

Good to know: Prebuilt packages include their runtime. Building and running your projects still requires their SDKs and package managers.


02. Open your first workspace

A workspace is the development folder where you review your everyday projects together. Select a root folder and DevWorkspace discovers supported project files within that scope.

1. Use File → Open or create workspace… or press Ctrl+O, then choose your development folder.
2. After scanning, inspect the project list and Overview. Review project type, folder and Git status where available.
3. Use the linking tools in File for a solution or folder in another location. Include linked projects in your existing workspace.
4. File changes are watched automatically. Press F5 to rescan manually and check the last successful scan time and any stale-data warning.

Good to know: Project discovery does not upload source code. Recognizing a technology does not imply every build and run operation is available for it.


03. Find projects and organize your work

Narrow a large project list to the work you need today. Favorites, groups and saved filters reduce repeated navigation.

1. Press Ctrl+F to focus project search. Select a project and inspect its information and available actions.
2. Favorite frequently used projects from the context menu. Organize related projects with groups and tags, using multi-selection for bulk grouping.
3. Save the current filter from View. Archive inactive projects and restore them when needed.
4. Open a project in its IDE using right-click → Open project/Open solution. Reach folders, documents and project tools from the same menu and choose a Visual Studio installation for supported solutions.

Good to know: Archiving does not delete source files. Showing or hiding component rows changes the list’s level of detail.


04. Review Git changes and create a commit

Check the branch and pending changes before starting work. Reviewing file diffs while preparing a commit makes it clear what you are about to send.

1. Select the project and open Git operations. Select a changed file to inspect its side-by-side diff.
2. Stage the files you want in the commit. Unstage a file to remove it from the index if necessary.
3. Write the message and choose Commit. Use the appropriate commit-and-push or separate push action when you also want to send it to the remote.
4. Use fetch to refresh remote information. Open history, branch/tag, remote, stash and worktree tools from the relevant Git menus.
5. Open View → Combined Git summary to review multiple repositories. Use the separate batch-fetch action in Git to fetch workspace repositories.

Good to know: The summary does not automatically fetch, pull or push. Ahead/behind reflects the last fetched state. Repository recovery is not a backup of local work that was never pushed.


05. Start a development setup with a profile

When an API, client and services are needed together, define a launch profile rather than preparing each one separately. Startup order and readiness rules are part of that setup.

1. With a workspace open, use File → Development hub or Ctrl+Shift+D. Open Edit profiles to prepare a profile.
2. Choose a project and action for each step. Arrange IDE, terminal, preset/custom command or eligible Compose startup actions in the required order.
3. Set a readiness port for a long-running service. Choose Wait for task completion for a build or setup task. Apply changes to the selected step when editing an existing one.
4. Use Check environment to review requirements. Prepare missing tools and, when appropriate, create a missing .env from an example and edit its local values yourself.
5. Choose Start development. Inspect failures or timeouts. Use Stop development to cancel pending startup and managed profile processes for the workspace.

Good to know: Port readiness checks TCP access on 127.0.0.1 rather than full application health. The default timeout is 60 seconds. A step without a readiness rule continues immediately.


06. Follow running applications and logs

See managed commands launched through DevWorkspace in one place. Review project, log and port information together to find the relevant process.

1. Open the list from the development hub or View → Running applications, then filter by project.
2. Inspect PID, state and TCP listening addresses. Search log text for the relevant output or error.
3. Select a supported file/line location and use Open file from log. VS Code opens the location when available; Notepad is the fallback.
4. Stop a command when needed and restart it after it has stopped. Use Operation Center for broader operation state and output.

Good to know: IDE and independent terminal windows are not part of the managed list. Managed commands stop when DevWorkspace closes; closing only the tool window does not stop them.


07. Check package security

Run a current scan first, then review the package and project context. Do not mistake an old report or failed scan for a clean result.

1. Use package security checks in Overview or the selected project’s Project tools → NuGet security. OSV-Scanner must be available for supported JavaScript/Dart lockfiles.
2. Start scanning. Review severity, affected package, version, project and target, and open the advisory when needed.
3. Read proposed changes when using supported repair or version-review flows. Consider direct/transitive dependencies and major-version changes before proceeding.
4. Inspect the follow-up scan. Run your project’s build and functional checks after package changes.

Good to know: Scanning and automatic repair have different coverage; not every package can be repaired automatically. Known-vulnerability scans do not guarantee application security.


08. Inspect documents, source and dependencies

README files, handoff notes and dependency context are useful starting points when returning to work. Use search and analysis tools to move from source files to related projects.

1. Open README and documents from the project’s context menu. Save where you left off and what comes next in its handoff note.
2. Press Ctrl+Shift+F for content search. Choose project scope and case sensitivity, then inspect plain-text matches with their file and line context.
3. Scan from View → Dependency and impact map. Select a project or service to inspect direct/indirect requirements and potentially affected projects.
4. Refresh project health and environment checks when needed. Pay attention to source files, skipped items and check times.

Good to know: Content search skips generated folders, local .env files, binaries and files larger than 2 MB. Dependency maps do not automatically resolve every runtime API relationship.


09. Comparison, move plans and templates

Comparing folder versions, reviewing move impacts and creating projects are separate tools. Choose the one that matches your task.

1. Select two project versions and open comparison from the context menu. Review changed or one-sided files and text diff previews.
2. If considering a project move, choose a destination inside the workspace in Move plan. Read reference and conflict findings.
3. In View → Project templates, choose a built-in or registered folder template. Set the project name and parent folder.
4. Review files with Preview, then choose Create. If the new folder is inside the scan scope, it appears after rescanning.

Good to know: Comparison does not merge files. Move planning is analysis only and does not move files. Templates do not overwrite existing targets or automatically install packages or create the initial commit.


10. Share a setup with your team

Development configuration and status reports serve different needs. One transfers a setup; the other shares the workspace’s last known state.

1. In Development hub → Team configuration, preview the configuration from profiles. Review project paths, commands, readiness rules and required tools.
2. Save the configuration as devworkspace.development.json in the workspace root. Include the file in your source repository if appropriate.
3. On another computer, open the same workspace, read the repository file, review its preview and import it. Importing does not execute commands.
4. To share only status, use HTML report export from File. Review the project-name inclusion option and inspect the file before sharing.

Good to know: Keep secrets in local .env files rather than shared configuration. Anonymous reports exclude local paths, branches, remotes and source code; workspace ZIP transfers have a different scope.


11. Prepare a release with Release Center

This section is for distributing supported .NET applications for Windows x64 through GitHub. Packages, source commits and remote drafts are verified together.

1. Right-click the project and open Release Center. Choose the correct application when a solution has multiple targets, and check project and GitHub origin.
2. Run preflight checks. Review tools, account, source state and verification projects. Complete Git preparation for a clean commit available on GitHub.
3. Prepare a stable version and release notes, optionally importing editable notes from commits. Choose Prepare package and follow operations in the isolated source copy.
4. Upload assets with Upload draft / resume. Review asset verification and relevant GitHub Actions results, then check repository, version and commit when confirming publication.
5. After publishing, refresh statistics from GitHub and export CSV when useful. Update download probes run in a test folder separate from the installed application.

Good to know: Packaging uses Debug. The target application needs Velopack integration for automatic updates. Download counts are not active or unique user counts.


12. Personalize the workspace and stay updated

Arrange frequent panels and your interface language around your daily routine. Keep release notes and help tools within reach.

1. Set the language in Settings and adjust theme, density and columns from View.
2. Open panels from Windows. Save a named layout, return to a saved layout later or restore the default.
3. Read current-version notes in Help → What’s New. In the installed copy, a ready update applies on the next launch or Restart now.
4. Use Help → Report a bug to prepare an editable GitHub draft. Add the problem and reproduction steps, then review before submitting.

Good to know: Bug reporting does not automatically submit an issue or attach logs. Optional local usage counters are off by default and never uploaded automatically.


13. Troubleshoot common situations

When an operation behaves unexpectedly, first check project scope, installed tools and the last check time.

1. Project missing: check the root folder and scan exclusions, confirm the file format is supported and refresh with F5.
2. Command unavailable: check project type and existing scripts. Confirm the required SDK or executable is available in Development tools.
3. GitHub operation failed: check GitHub CLI installation, authentication, repository access and origin.
4. Profile will not start: refresh environment checks and inspect missing .env keys, port conflicts, failed tasks or readiness timeouts.
5. Results look old: read the last scan/check time. Rerun the relevant operation after resolving tool or network issues rather than treating an old report as new.


14. Quick keyboard access

These shortcuts cover frequent daily actions. See the application’s Help menu for other shortcuts.

1. Ctrl+O — Open or create a workspace.
2. Ctrl+K — Open the command palette.
3. Ctrl+F — Search the project list.
4. Ctrl+Shift+F — Open cross-project content search.
5. Ctrl+Shift+D — Open the development hub.
6. F5 — Rescan the workspace.
